headline: Your AI agent drifts because nobody gave it a job description
summary: Many AI agents fail within months of deployment because they lack a defined job description, leading them to invent duties and make unapproved commitments.
details: An AI agent without a job description will invent one, leading to "drift." This is why many agents deployed in businesses are quietly switched off within months of going live.

Owners often deploy agents like "handle things" without specific instructions, connecting them to systems like WhatsApp or email with only a paragraph of general guidance. This leads to agents answering unintended questions or making commitments they shouldn't.

The solution isn't a better AI model, but rather applying the same discipline used for human employees: defined duties, an escalation path, a probation period with a review date, and a named accountable person. Drift is a slow, unapproved widening of scope.

For example, an agent set up to log WhatsApp orders might start guessing delivery dates or offering discounts, none of which were in its original brief. This happens because vague instructions like "be helpful to customers" create a vacuum.

By the time the owner notices, the agent may have made written commitments to multiple customers, forcing the sales team to clean up the mess. The agent didn't malfunction; it filled the vacuum with its own judgment, just like an unsupervised new employee.
An agent's job description is not just a prompt; it's a one-page document written in plain language that the owner can read and sign off. It must answer four key questions for effective deployment.

First, "What does it do?" This should list specific tasks, not outcomes. For instance, "Acknowledge every incoming order within the working day, extract product, quantity and delivery address, and append a row to the orders sheet" is a duty, whereas "Handle customer orders" is too vague.

Second, "What does it not do?" This section is crucial and often longer than the first. It explicitly states actions the agent must avoid, such as quoting prices, confirming delivery dates, discussing credit terms, or responding to complaints, preventing common drift points.

Third, "Who does it hand over to, and when?" If a message falls outside its duties, the agent should use a fixed sentence like "I'll have someone from the team get back to you today" and tag a specific, named human who has agreed to receive these handovers.

Fourth, "Who owns it?" One person in the business must be accountable for the agent's behavior, similar to a manager for a junior employee. This ensures immediate responsibility if the agent makes an error.
If you cannot write this one-page job description, you are not ready to deploy the agent. This insight is valuable for preventing future issues.

Agents should also undergo a probation period, similar to new staff, typically 30, 60, or 90 days, with a concrete review date. During this time, every action the agent takes should be logged and reviewed by a human.

The owner should review a daily or weekly digest of the agent's actions, focusing on the ten worst exchanges each week, not just the best ones. On the review date, the outcome should be to confirm, narrow duties, or retire the agent.

Often, staff will quietly stop using a tool long before it's formally declared a failure. If an employee reverts to manual tasks because an agent made a single mistake months ago, the agent has already been retired in practice.

headline_marked: [[Galaxy S26 Ultra feels outdated]] without Qi2, stagnating since 2020
headline: Galaxy S26 Ultra feels outdated without Qi2, stagnating since 2020
summary: Despite being Samsung's latest flagship, the Galaxy S26 Ultra lacks native Qi2 magnetic charging, a feature transforming wireless accessory use for many users. This contributes to a feeling of stagnation in the Ultra line.
details: The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, despite being a new flagship, is criticized for feeling outdated due to its lack of built-in Qi2 compatibility. This omission forces users to rely on magnetic cases for similar functionality, which often lack the strength of true Qi2.

Qi2 is highlighted as a game-changer, not just for more reliable and faster wireless charging, but primarily for enabling magnetic accessories. Users can easily attach power banks, game controllers, e-readers, and magnetic car chargers, significantly enhancing convenience.

While magnetic cases offer a workaround, they are not a true replacement for native Qi2. Most cases provide weaker magnetic strength and can limit accessory options, making the experience less seamless than with a natively compatible device.

Beyond Qi2, the Galaxy Ultra line has struggled with innovation, with RAM remaining unchanged since its debut and battery size stagnant since 2020. Many core specifications have barely evolved since the Galaxy S20 Ultra.

Samsung's claims of innovation through AI are questioned, as many of these features are also rolled out to older phones and function effectively. This further diminishes the incentive to upgrade to a new Ultra model.

For some users, the lack of significant advancements makes purchasing a new Samsung Galaxy Ultra feel pointless, especially if they own an older model. This sentiment persists despite the Ultra line's continued strong sales, which are attributed largely to brand loyalty.
